content: 1. Core capacities for health regulations include the development of skills among national and international health workers, particularly in humanitarian settings and during public health emergencies. 2. Guidance is available on financing lifelong learning systems to strengthen priority health and social workforce cadres, including community-based health workers, and to achieve integrated, people-centered care. 3. Transformative education is a key concept, with data reporting on an annual basis. Potential data sources include integrated financial management systems from ministries such as Finance, Health, Education, and Defense, as well as education management information systems and national statistics bureaus. 4. Expenditure per graduate in health workforce education and training programs is calculated by dividing the total expenditure on health workforce education by the total number of graduates. This can be disaggregated by program type and institutional ownership (public or private). 5. Recurrent costs of specialist medical education per graduate are determined by dividing the total cost of specialist medical education by the number of graduates from these programs. This can be further broken down by specialty and public/private sector. 6. The cost of qualified educators per graduate is calculated by dividing the total recurrent costs of qualified educators by the number of graduates from health workforce education and training programs. 7. Total expenditure on in-service training and continuing professional development is tracked annually, with potential data sources including financial management systems, education management systems, and national health accounts. 8. Module 5 of the National Health Workforce Accounts addresses entries into and exits from the health labor market, as well as labor market imbalances. Indicators differentiate between domestic efforts and reliance on foreign health workers, and monitor both voluntary and involuntary exits. 9. The ratio of previous year graduates who started practice within one year of graduation is calculated by dividing the number of such graduates by the total number of graduates from the previous year. This can be disaggregated by occupation and sex. 10. The replenishment rate from domestic efforts is the ratio of newly active domestically trained health workers to the total stock of active health workers. Only domestically trained workers are included, and data should reflect mid-year or end-of-year counts. 11. The entry rate of foreign health workers is the percentage of newly active foreign-trained health workers relative to the total stock of active health workers. In the absence of data on foreign-trained workers, foreign-born health workers starting practice can be used. 12. The voluntary exit rate from the health labor market is the ratio of active health workers who leave the sector voluntarily (e.g., emigration, temporary leave, sector change, early retirement) to the total stock of active health workers. Early retirement is considered voluntary, while standard-age retirement is not. 13. The involuntary exit rate from the health labor market is the ratio of active health workers who leave due to reasons such as death, standard-age retirement, suspension, or long-term illness to the total stock of active health workers. Early retirement is excluded from this indicator. 14. The unemployment rate among trained health workers is calculated as the number of unemployed health workers divided by the total number of active and unemployed health workers in the labor force. This can be disaggregated by occupation, sex, and subnational level.
